title: Everything is running away
teaches: How the redshifts of galaxies showed the universe is expanding, why that doesn't put us at the centre, and how the expansion gives the universe an age

blocks.text: In 1912, years before anyone knew what the spiral nebulae were, Vesto Slipher at the Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff, Arizona, set out to measure how fast they were moving. It was miserable work. A spiral is so faint that to spread its light into a spectrum he had to keep the telescope pointed at it for twenty, thirty, or forty hours, over several nights, on the same photographic plate. But a spectrum shows dark lines, and as *What the stars are made of* showed, the lines of something coming towards you are shifted to the blue and the lines of something going away are shifted to the red. The size of the shift gives the speed.

His first target was the Andromeda nebula. Its lines were shifted to the blue: it was coming towards us at 300 kilometres a second, faster than any star then known. Then he tried others, and the pattern turned round. By 1917 he had measured twenty-five spirals, and twenty-one were moving away, some at over a thousand kilometres a second. The redshifts kept coming. Andromeda, it turned out, was the exception, a near neighbour falling towards us. Nearly everything else was running away.

Once Hubble had shown, in *Island universes*, that the spirals were galaxies and found ways to estimate their distances, the obvious thing was to put the two together. The first to do it was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist who had served as an artillery officer in the First World War. In 1927 he showed that Einstein's general relativity allowed a universe that expands, and that in such a universe galaxies should recede at speeds in proportion to their distances. He took Slipher's speeds and Hubble's distances and found roughly that. He published it in French, in a little-read Belgian journal, and almost nobody noticed.[^lemaitre-einstein]

Two years later Hubble, working with his assistant Milton Humason,[^humason] published a graph of the galaxies' speeds against their distances. The points scattered, but they lay along a straight line: a galaxy twice as far away recedes twice as fast. It became famous as Hubble's law. When Lemaître's paper was translated into English in 1931, the passage with his own estimate of the rate was missing, which for decades looked like someone suppressing his priority. In 2011 the letters turned up: Lemaître had cut it himself, because Hubble's newer figures were better. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union voted to call it the Hubble–Lemaître law.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Galaxies are receding from us at speeds in proportion to their distances: the universe is expanding.

blocks.text: Every distant galaxy is moving away from us, which makes us look suspiciously like the centre of the universe. Try looking from somewhere else.

blocks.caption: A patch of galaxies stretched evenly, seen from the galaxy you call home. The faint dots are where they started. On the right, each galaxy's speed away from home against its distance.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then stretch the patch and look from each of three homes

blocks.text: When a pattern stretches evenly, every point sees every other point moving away, and the further one moving faster. The straight line on the graph is what even stretching looks like from anywhere. So the expansion has no centre, and nothing to expand into. Galaxies are not flying out from one spot into empty space; the distances between galaxies are growing, everywhere at once. (Galaxies themselves don't stretch: gravity holds them together, as it holds the Solar System. So do clusters of galaxies. It is the gaps between them that grow.)

Two consequences follow. First, the most distant galaxies are receding faster than light. That breaks no rule: the speed limit of *Muons that live too long* is for things moving through space, and here it is space itself that stretches. Second, the redshift of a distant galaxy isn't really a Doppler shift. Its light was stretched along with space on its long way here; the longer the travel time, the more it has been stretched. For nearby galaxies the two ways of thinking give the same answer, which is why Slipher's method worked.

parts.title: A universe younger than its rocks

blocks.text: If the galaxies are flying apart, then run the film backwards and they were once together. At a steady rate, the time since then is just distance divided by speed. Hubble's rate, in our units, was that galaxies a million light years further away recede about 150 km/s faster. Run that back and everything was together about two billion years ago.

That was a problem, because by then geologists were dating rocks by their radioactivity, as in Geology's *How old is the Earth?*, and the oldest were already coming out at two to three billion years. A universe can't be younger than the rocks in it. Some astronomers took this as a reason to doubt the whole idea of an expanding universe.

blocks.caption: The age of a universe that has always expanded at a steady rate, against the age of the Earth and its oldest crystals.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then bring the expansion rate down to today's value

blocks.text: The mistake was in the distances. During the Second World War, the blackout in Los Angeles gave Walter Baade, a German-born astronomer barred from war work, unusually dark skies at Mount Wilson. He found that stars come in two broad families, younger ones in the discs of galaxies and older ones in their central bulges and in globular clusters. By 1952 he had shown that each family has its own kind of Cepheid: Hubble's Cepheids in Andromeda were the brighter kind, measured against a ruler made with the fainter kind, though the ruler's zero point was actually off for both. Either way, every distance beyond our galaxy roughly doubled and the expansion rate halved. Beyond the reach of Cepheids, Hubble had used a galaxy's brightest stars as a yardstick; through the 1950s Allan Sandage showed that many of those points of light were whole glowing gas clouds and star clusters, which multiplied the distances several times more. The universe was at last older than the Earth.

Today the expansion rate, measured many ways, gives an **age of the universe** of 13.8 billion years: the time since everything was crowded together, hot and dense. (The careful figure allows for the rate having changed over time, which is the story of *The speeding universe*.) The Sun and the Earth, at 4.6 billion, are a third that age.

The expansion rate is now known to a few per cent, which is where a new puzzle has appeared. Measured close to home, with Cepheids and exploding stars as standard candles, it comes out at about 22 kilometres a second faster for each million light years further away.[^hubble-units] Worked out from the afterglow of the early universe (*Why is the night sky dark?*), assuming our best description of what the universe contains, it comes out at about 20.5. The difference is small, but both teams say their errors are smaller still. This is called the Hubble tension, and it is unsettled. It may be a hidden mistake in one of the measurements, or a sign that something is missing from our picture of the universe. New telescopes are checking both.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the expanding universe
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Galaxy X is 200 million light years away and recedes at 4,300 km/s. Galaxy Y is 600 million light years away. About how fast does Y recede?
items.why: Three times as far, three times as fast: that is the Hubble–Lemaître law.

items.ask: An astronomer in a galaxy a billion light years away measures the speeds of galaxies around her. What does she find?
choices: They all recede from her, faster the further they are
They all recede from us, not from her
items.why: Even stretching looks the same from every point. There is no centre.

items.ask: Slipher's first spiral, Andromeda, was approaching at 300 km/s. Why doesn't that contradict the expansion?
choices: It is a near neighbour, pulled towards us by gravity
The universe is shrinking near us
items.why: Galaxies close together are held by gravity, like stars in a galaxy. The expansion shows up in the gaps between distant galaxies.

items.ask: The most distant galaxies recede faster than light. Why is that allowed?
choices: Space itself is stretching; nothing is moving through space faster than light
items.why: Light's speed is a limit on motion through space. The growth of the distances between galaxies isn't that kind of motion.

items.ask: Hubble's 1929 rate gave a universe of 2 billion years, younger than Earth's rocks. What fixed it?
choices: Baade found two kinds of Cepheid, which began a series of corrections that multiplied the distances to galaxies
The rocks were dated again and found younger
The universe was found to be shrinking
items.why: With greater distances, the same speeds mean a slower rate, so a longer time since everything was together.

choices: Two good ways of measuring the expansion rate disagree slightly
Hubble and Lemaître argued about credit
Galaxies are being pulled apart by expansion
items.why: Measurements nearby give about 22 km/s per million light years; the early universe gives about 20.5. It is unsettled.

summary: **Nearly every galaxy is redshifted.** Slipher from 1912: most spirals are moving away (Andromeda, a neighbour, is approaching).
**The farther, the faster.** Lemaître (1927) and Hubble (1929): recession speed grows in step with distance. The universe is expanding.
**No centre.** Even stretching looks the same from every galaxy; it is the distances between galaxies that grow.
**Space stretches.** Faster-than-light recession breaks no rule; the redshift is light stretched on its journey.
**The expansion gives an age.** Hubble's distances were too small (two kinds of Cepheid, 1952); today the universe is 13.8 billion years old.
**The Hubble tension.** Nearby measurements give about 22 km/s per million light years, the early universe about 20.5; still unsettled.

lemaitre-einstein.title: Einstein's verdict
lemaitre-einstein.text: Lemaître met Einstein at the Solvay Conference in Brussels in October 1927 and handed him the paper. Einstein had read it already. The mathematics was sound, he told Lemaître, "but from the physical point of view it looks to me abominable." Like almost everyone then, Einstein still wanted the universe to be static.

humason.title: From mule driver to astronomer
humason.text: Milton Humason dropped out of school at fourteen and began at Mount Wilson in 1917 driving mule teams up the trail with building supplies for the 100-inch telescope. He became the observatory's janitor, then a night assistant, and turned out to be so patient and deft at guiding the big telescope through multiday exposures that Hubble made him his collaborator.

hubble-units.title: Astronomers' units for the rate
hubble-units.text: Astronomers measure large distances in megaparsecs, where one megaparsec is 3.26 million light years. In those units, the two values of the Hubble constant are about 73 and 67 kilometres per second per megaparsec.
